statement: Let $X$ be a [compact](c:compact-space) [metric space](c:metric-space) and $\mathcal{F}$ a family of [continuous](c:continuous-function) functions $X \to \mathbb{R}$. Every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ has a [uniformly convergent](c:uniform-convergence) subsequence if and only if $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly bounded and [equicontinuous](c:equicontinuity).

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is a [compact](c:compact-space) metric space.
Every member of $\mathcal{F}$ is a [continuous](c:continuous-function) function $X \to \mathbb{R}$.

conclusion: The family $\mathcal{F}$ is uniformly bounded and [equicontinuous](c:equicontinuity) exactly when every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ has a subsequence that converges uniformly on $X$.

formal.difference: The declaration proves only sufficiency, for bounded continuous maps from a compact space into a metric space with all values in one compact set, and it concludes that the closure of the family is compact. Necessity and the subsequence form are not stated.

proofs.name: Total boundedness
proofs.slogan: Discretize the family by finitely many sample points and values, so that its closure is totally bounded and complete, hence compact.
proofs.scope: Both directions: steps 1 to 5 prove sufficiency and step 6 proves necessity. An empty $X$ or an empty family satisfies both sides trivially.

roles.why: [Compactness](c:compact-space) of $X$ gives the finite cover of step 1 and the uniform continuity of step 6.
Continuity puts $\mathcal{F}$ in the complete space $C(X)$ with the sup metric.

steps.slogan: Cover $X$ by finitely many open sets on which each member varies by less than $\varepsilon$.
steps.detail: Fix $\varepsilon > 0$. [Equicontinuity](c:equicontinuity) gives each $x$ an open neighborhood $U_x$ with $|f(y) - f(z)| < \varepsilon$ for all $y, z \in U_x$ and all $f \in \mathcal{F}$. Compactness keeps finitely many sets $U_{x_1}, \dots, U_{x_m}$ that cover $X$.

steps.slogan: Pick finitely many values $y_1, \dots, y_k$ that are $\varepsilon$-dense in the common range $[-M, M]$.
steps.detail: Uniform boundedness gives $M$ with $|f(x)| \le M$ for all $f \in \mathcal{F}$ and $x \in X$. The compact interval $[-M, M]$ has a finite subset $\{y_1, \dots, y_k\}$ within $\varepsilon$ of each of its points.

steps.slogan: Show that two members with the same finite code lie within $4\varepsilon$ of each other.
steps.detail: Give $f$ the code $i \mapsto j$ with $|f(x_i) - y_j| < \varepsilon$; there are at most $k^m$ codes. If $f$ and $g$ share a code and $x \in U_{x_i}$, then $|f(x) - g(x)| \le |f(x) - f(x_i)| + |f(x_i) - g(x_i)| + |g(x_i) - g(x)| < 4\varepsilon$. So $\mathcal{F}$ and its closure are [totally bounded](c:totally-bounded-space).

steps.slogan: Show that the closure of $\mathcal{F}$ in $C(X)$ is complete.
steps.detail: In $C(X)$ with the sup metric, a Cauchy sequence converges uniformly to a function that is continuous by the uniform limit theorem. So $C(X)$ is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space), and its closed subset $\overline{\mathcal{F}}$ is complete.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the closure is compact and extract a uniformly convergent subsequence.
steps.detail: A complete and totally bounded metric space is compact, and a compact metric space is sequentially compact. So every sequence in $\mathcal{F}$ has a subsequence that converges in the sup metric, which is uniform convergence.

steps.slogan: Prove the converse from a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $\mathcal{F}$.
steps.detail: If every sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence, $\mathcal{F}$ has no infinite $\varepsilon$-separated sequence, so it has a finite $\varepsilon$-net $f_1, \dots, f_n$. Then $|f| \le \max_i \sup|f_i| + \varepsilon$ for all $f$. Each $f_i$ is uniformly continuous on compact $X$, and a common $\delta$ gives $|f(y) - f(z)| < 3\varepsilon$ whenever $d(y, z) < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 5 show that a uniformly bounded equicontinuous family has uniformly convergent subsequences. Step 6 shows the converse, so the two conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of $X$ makes finitely many sample points suffice.
concepts.c:metric-space: The metric on $X$ measures closeness in the equicontinuity estimates.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity places the family inside the complete space $C(X)$.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Convergence in the sup metric is exactly uniform convergence.
concepts.c:equicontinuity: Equicontinuity gives one neighborhood that works for all members at once.
concepts.c:totally-bounded-space: Finitely many codes make the closure totally bounded.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness of $C(X)$ supplies the limits of Cauchy subsequences.

proofs.name: Diagonal subsequence
proofs.slogan: Make a subsequence converge on a countable dense set by a diagonal argument, then spread the convergence over $X$ by equicontinuity.
proofs.scope: Both directions: steps 1 to 4 build the subsequence of a given sequence, and step 5 proves necessity. An empty $X$ is trivial.

roles.why: [Compactness](c:compact-space) gives a countable dense set, uniform equicontinuity and the finite net of step 5.
Continuity of the members gives their uniform continuity in step 5.

steps.slogan: Choose a countable [dense set](c:dense-set) $\{q_1, q_2, \dots\}$ in $X$.
steps.detail: For each $k$, compactness covers $X$ by finitely many balls of radius $1/k$. The centers of all these balls, over all $k$, form a countable dense set.

steps.slogan: Extract a diagonal subsequence that converges at every point $q_j$.
steps.detail: Uniform boundedness and the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem give a subsequence of $(f_n)$ that converges at $q_1$, a further one that converges at $q_2$, and so on. The diagonal sequence $g_k$, the $k$-th term of the $k$-th subsequence, converges at every $q_j$.

steps.slogan: Show by [equicontinuity](c:equicontinuity) that the diagonal sequence is uniformly Cauchy.
steps.detail: On compact $X$ equicontinuity is uniform, so some $\delta$ gives $|f(x) - f(y)| < \varepsilon$ for $d(x, y) < \delta$ and all $f \in \mathcal{F}$. Finitely many $q_j$ are $\delta$-dense, and for large $k, l$ the values $g_k(q_j)$ and $g_l(q_j)$ differ by less than $\varepsilon$ there. Hence $|g_k(x) - g_l(x)| < 3\varepsilon$ for every $x$.

steps.slogan: Take the pointwise limit and show that the convergence is uniform.
steps.detail: Each sequence $(g_k(x))$ is a Cauchy sequence of reals, so it converges to some $g(x)$. Letting $l \to \infty$ in step 3 gives $|g_k(x) - g(x)| \le 3\varepsilon$ for all $x$ and all large $k$, so $g_k \to g$ uniformly.

steps.slogan: Prove the converse from a finite $\varepsilon$-net of $\mathcal{F}$.
steps.detail: If every sequence has a uniformly convergent subsequence, $\mathcal{F}$ has no infinite $\varepsilon$-separated sequence, so it has a finite $\varepsilon$-net $f_1, \dots, f_n$. Then $|f| \le \max_i \sup|f_i| + \varepsilon$ for all $f$. Each $f_i$ is uniformly continuous on compact $X$, and a common $\delta$ gives $|f(y) - f(z)| < 3\varepsilon$ whenever $d(y, z) < \delta$.

steps.slogan: Join the two directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Steps 1 to 4 give a uniformly convergent subsequence of every sequence in a uniformly bounded equicontinuous family. Step 5 shows the converse, so the two conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of $X$ makes finitely many sample points suffice.
concepts.c:metric-space: The metric on $X$ measures closeness in the equicontinuity estimates.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity places the family inside the complete space $C(X)$.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: Convergence in the sup metric is exactly uniform convergence.
concepts.c:equicontinuity: Equicontinuity gives one neighborhood that works for all members at once.
concepts.c:dense-set: Convergence on a dense set spreads to all of $X$.

source.note: The classical diagonal proof, as in W. Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., theorems 7.23 and 7.25.

statement: Assuming the [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice), every [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $K$ has a [basis](c:basis-of-a-vector-space): a [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) subset that spans $V$.

hypotheses.text: $V$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) over a field $K$.
The [axiom of choice](c:axiom-of-choice) holds.

conclusion: Some subset $B \subseteq V$ is linearly independent and spans $V$.

proofs.name: Maximal independent set
proofs.slogan: Take a maximal linearly independent set by Zorn's lemma and show that maximality forces it to span the space.
proofs.scope: Every vector space, of any dimension; for $V = \{0\}$ the basis is the empty set. The converse, that the theorem implies the axiom of choice (Blass 1984), is not proved here.

roles.why: Choice gives Zorn's lemma, which supplies the maximal independent set.
Division by a nonzero scalar $c \in K$ shows that an independent set extends by any vector outside its span.

steps.slogan: Order the linearly independent subsets of $V$ by inclusion.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of linearly independent subsets of $V$, a [partial order](c:partial-order) under $\subseteq$. It is nonempty, because the empty set is linearly independent.

steps.slogan: Bound every [chain](c:chain) of independent sets by its union.
steps.detail: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a chain in $\mathcal{P}$ and $U = \bigcup \mathcal{C}$. A finite subset of $U$ lies in one member of $\mathcal{C}$, because the chain is totally ordered, so it is linearly independent. Hence $U \in \mathcal{P}$ is an upper bound of $\mathcal{C}$.

steps.slogan: Take a [maximal](c:maximal-element) independent set $B$ by Zorn's lemma.
steps.detail: Zorn's lemma follows from the axiom of choice and applies to the nonempty poset $\mathcal{P}$, in which every chain has an upper bound. It gives $B \in \mathcal{P}$ that no strictly larger independent set contains.

steps.slogan: Show that every vector of $V$ lies in the span of $B$.
steps.detail: Let $v \notin \operatorname{span} B$ and suppose $c v + \sum_i c_i b_i = 0$. If $c \ne 0$, then $v = -c^{-1} \sum_i c_i b_i \in \operatorname{span} B$, which is false; so $c = 0$ and then all $c_i = 0$. So $B \cup \{v\}$ is independent and strictly larger than $B$, against maximality.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the maximal set $B$ is a basis of $V$.
steps.detail: The set $B$ is linearly independent by step 3 and spans $V$ by step 4, so it is a basis. For $V = \{0\}$ the result is $B = \emptyset$.

concepts.c:axiom-of-choice: Choice is the source of Zorn's lemma in this proof.
concepts.c:vector-space: The span and independence are taken inside the vector space.
concepts.c:basis-of-a-vector-space: The maximal independent set is the basis that the theorem asks for.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independent subsets are the objects that Zorn's lemma orders.
concepts.c:partial-order: Inclusion orders the independent sets so that Zorn's lemma applies.
concepts.c:chain: Every chain must have an upper bound for Zorn's lemma.
concepts.c:maximal-element: Maximality forbids any vector outside the span.

source.note: The standard Zorn's lemma argument, as in S. Lang, Algebra, chapter III, section 5.

hypotheses.text: The terms lie in the [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ of finite dimension $n$.
The sequence $(x_k)$ is [bounded](c:bounded-set): $\|x_k\| \le M$ for all $k$.

conclusion: Some subsequence $(x_{k_j})$ converges to a point $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\|a\| \le M$.

formal.difference: The declaration works in any proper metric space, such as $\mathbb{R}^n$, and needs the terms to lie in a bounded set $s$ only for infinitely many indices. It also puts the limit in the closure of $s$.

proofs.name: Compact closed ball
proofs.slogan: Put the terms in a closed ball, which is compact by the Heine–Borel theorem, and extract a subsequence that converges to a cluster point.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem for every $n \ge 0$; for $n = 0$ the sequence is constant.

roles.why: Boundedness puts every term in the closed ball $\bar B(0, M)$.
Finite dimension makes the closed ball compact by the Heine–Borel theorem.

steps.slogan: Place every term in the closed ball $\bar B(0, M)$.
steps.detail: Boundedness gives $M$ with $\|x_k\| \le M$ for all $k$. The ball $\bar B(0, M)$ is a [closed](c:closed-set) and bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ that contains every term.

steps.slogan: Show by the Heine–Borel theorem that the closed ball is [compact](c:compact-space).
steps.detail: In the finite-dimensional space $\mathbb{R}^n$, every closed and bounded set is compact. So the ball $\bar B(0, M)$ is compact.

steps.slogan: Find a point of the ball whose every neighborhood holds infinitely many terms.
steps.detail: Suppose each point $y$ of the ball has an open neighborhood $V_y$ with $x_k \in V_y$ for only finitely many $k$. Finitely many $V_y$ cover the compact ball, so only finitely many indices exist, which is false. So some $a \in \bar B(0, M)$ has infinitely many terms in each ball $B(a, 1/j)$.

steps.slogan: Choose increasing indices $k_j$ with $x_{k_j}$ in the ball $B(a, 1/j)$.
steps.detail: Pick $k_1$ with $x_{k_1} \in B(a, 1)$ and then $k_{j+1} > k_j$ with $x_{k_{j+1}} \in B(a, 1/(j+1))$, which exists by step 3. Then $\|x_{k_j} - a\| < 1/j \to 0$, so the subsequence converges to $a$, and $\|a\| \le M$.

concepts.c:bounded-set: Boundedness keeps the terms in one bounded region.
concepts.c:sequence: The theorem concerns an arbitrary sequence of points.
concepts.c:subsequence: The proof builds the convergent subsequence explicitly.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: Finite dimension is what makes bounded sequences behave well.
concepts.c:closed-set: A closed ball keeps the limit point inside it.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the ball gives the finite subcover.

source.note: mathlib takes the compact closure of the bounded set in a proper space (Bornology.IsBounded.isCompact_closure) and extracts the subsequence by sequential compactness (IsCompact.isSeqCompact, IsSeqCompact.subseq_of_frequently_in).

proofs.name: Monotone subsequence
proofs.slogan: Extract a monotone subsequence in each coordinate in turn, and let the completeness of the reals give each coordinate a limit.
proofs.scope: Steps 1 and 2 prove the case $n = 1$; step 3 extends it to $\mathbb{R}^n$ one coordinate at a time.

roles.why: Each coordinate sequence is bounded by $M$, so its monotone subsequences converge.
Finitely many coordinates need only finitely many successive extractions.

steps.slogan: Find a [monotone](c:monotone-sequence) subsequence of a real sequence by its peaks.
steps.detail: Call $m$ a peak of $(t_k)$ if $t_m \ge t_k$ for all $k > m$. Infinitely many peaks give a non-increasing subsequence. With finitely many peaks, every index after the last peak has a later index with a larger value, which gives an increasing subsequence.

steps.slogan: Show that a bounded monotone real sequence converges to its supremum or infimum.
steps.detail: If $(t_k)$ increases and is bounded, the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) $s$ exists by completeness of the reals. Some $t_K > s - \varepsilon$, and then $s - \varepsilon < t_k \le s$ for all $k \ge K$; the non-increasing case is symmetric.

steps.slogan: Repeat the extraction for the coordinates $1, \dots, n$ in turn.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give a subsequence whose first coordinates converge. A further subsequence makes the second coordinates converge, and the first still converge, because a subsequence of a convergent sequence has the same limit. After $n$ extractions every coordinate converges.

steps.slogan: Conclude that the final subsequence converges in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
steps.detail: Convergence in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is convergence of each coordinate, so the final subsequence converges to the point $a$ of coordinate limits. The norm is continuous, so $\|a\| \le M$.

concepts.c:bounded-set: Boundedness keeps the terms in one bounded region.
concepts.c:sequence: The theorem concerns an arbitrary sequence of points.
concepts.c:subsequence: The proof builds the convergent subsequence explicitly.
concepts.c:euclidean-space: Finite dimension is what makes bounded sequences behave well.
concepts.c:monotone-sequence: Every real sequence has a monotone subsequence, which then converges.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum is the limit of an increasing bounded sequence.

source.note: The peak argument for monotone subsequences with the monotone convergence theorem, as in R. G. Bartle and D. R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis, section 3.4.

statement: Let $(a_n)$ be a sequence in a [Banach space](c:banach-space), such as $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. The [series](c:series) $\sum_n a_n$ converges if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $\|a_{m+1} + \dots + a_n\| < \varepsilon$ for all $n > m \ge N$.

hypotheses.text: The terms lie in a [Banach space](c:banach-space), that is a [complete](c:complete-metric-space) normed space.

conclusion: The [partial sums](c:partial-sum) $s_n = a_1 + \dots + a_n$ converge exactly when the block sums $a_{m+1} + \dots + a_n$ become uniformly small.

formal.difference: The declaration treats a family indexed by any type in a complete commutative topological group and uses the net of sums over finite index sets. It therefore characterizes unconditional summability, not convergence of the ordered partial sums $s_n$.

proofs.name: Cauchy partial sums
proofs.slogan: Write block sums as differences of partial sums, then use that a sequence in a complete space converges exactly when it is Cauchy.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the forward direction holds in every normed space, and only the backward direction needs completeness.

roles.why: Completeness turns the Cauchy sequence of partial sums into a convergent one.

steps.slogan: Write each block sum as a difference of two [partial sums](c:partial-sum).
steps.detail: Let $s_n = a_1 + \dots + a_n$. Then $a_{m+1} + \dots + a_n = s_n - s_m$ for $n > m$, so the condition says exactly that $(s_n)$ is a [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence).

steps.slogan: Show that convergent partial sums form a Cauchy sequence.
steps.detail: If $s_n \to s$, choose $N$ with $\|s_n - s\| < \varepsilon/2$ for $n \ge N$. Then $\|s_n - s_m\| \le \|s_n - s\| + \|s - s_m\| < \varepsilon$ for $n > m \ge N$.

steps.slogan: Take the limit of the Cauchy partial sums in the complete space.
steps.detail: If $(s_n)$ is a Cauchy sequence, the completeness of the Banach space gives a limit $s$. So the series converges, with sum $s$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the stated criterion.
steps.detail: By step 1 the condition is the Cauchy property of $(s_n)$. Steps 2 and 3 show that this property is equivalent to convergence of $(s_n)$, which is convergence of the series.

concepts.c:banach-space: The terms live in a normed space where Cauchy sequences converge.
concepts.c:series: Convergence of a series means convergence of its partial sums.
concepts.c:complete-metric-space: Completeness supplies the limit of the Cauchy partial sums.
concepts.c:partial-sum: Block sums are differences of two partial sums.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The criterion is the Cauchy property of the partial sums.

source.note: mathlib proves it as cauchy_map_iff_exists_tendsto: in a complete space a filter map is Cauchy exactly when it converges; the proof uses the same step for the sequence of partial sums.

statement: If $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) and a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ divides $|G|$, then $G$ has an element of [order](c:order-of-an-element) $p$.

hypotheses.text: $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group).
$p$ is a [prime number](c:prime-number).
$p$ divides the order $|G|$.

conclusion: Some $x \in G$ satisfies $x^p = e$ and $x \ne e$, so $x$ has [order](c:order-of-an-element) exactly $p$.

proofs.name: McKay's rotation count
proofs.slogan: Rotate the $p$-tuples with product $e$, count the fixed tuples modulo $p$, and find a constant tuple other than $(e, \dots, e)$.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; $|G| \ge p \ge 2$ holds automatically because $p$ divides $|G| \ge 1$.

roles.why: Finiteness makes the tuple set $X$ finite with $|X| = |G|^{p-1}$.
Primality limits the orbit sizes to $1$ and $p$ and gives order exactly $p$.
Divisibility of $|G|$ by $p$ gives $p \mid |X|$.

steps.slogan: Count the $p$-tuples of group elements whose product is $e$.
steps.detail: Let $X = \{(x_1, \dots, x_p) \in G^p : x_1 x_2 \cdots x_p = e\}$. The entries $x_1, \dots, x_{p-1}$ are free and determine $x_p$, so $|X| = |G|^{p-1}$, which $p$ divides.

steps.slogan: Let $\mathbb{Z}/p$ act on these tuples by cyclic rotation.
steps.detail: If $x_1 (x_2 \cdots x_p) = e$, then $(x_2 \cdots x_p) x_1 = e$, because a left inverse in a group is a right inverse. So rotation maps $X$ to $X$, and $p$ rotations give the identity, which defines a [group action](c:group-action) of $\mathbb{Z}/p$.

steps.slogan: Show that every [orbit](c:orbit) of the rotation has $1$ or $p$ elements.
steps.detail: By the class formula an orbit is in bijection with the cosets of a stabilizer in $\mathbb{Z}/p$, so its size divides $p$ by Lagrange's theorem. Since $p$ is prime, the size is $1$ or $p$.

steps.slogan: Count the tuples fixed by rotation modulo $p$.
steps.detail: The orbits partition $X$, so $|X|$ is congruent modulo $p$ to the number of one-point orbits. A tuple fixed by rotation is constant, $(x, \dots, x)$ with $x^p = e$. Since $p \mid |X|$, $p$ divides the number of such $x$.

steps.slogan: Find a fixed tuple $(x, \dots, x)$ with $x \ne e$.
steps.detail: The tuple $(e, \dots, e)$ is fixed, so the number of fixed tuples is a positive multiple of $p$, at least $p \ge 2$. So some $x \ne e$ has $x^p = e$; its order divides $p$ and is not $1$, so it equals $p$.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness makes the counts and the induction possible.
concepts.c:prime-number: Only a prime forces orbit sizes or indices to behave this way.
concepts.c:order-of-an-element: The goal is an element whose order is exactly $p$.
concepts.c:group-action: Rotation of tuples is an action of $\mathbb{Z}/p$.
concepts.c:orbit: Orbit sizes $1$ or $p$ give the count modulo $p$.

source.note: mathlib counts vectorsProdEqOne G p (VectorsProdEqOne.card), rotates the vectors, gets a second fixed point from exists_fixed_point_of_prime' and finishes with orderOf_eq_prime.

proofs.name: Induction through the class equation
proofs.slogan: Prove the abelian case through a quotient, then reduce a general group to a proper centralizer or to its center by the class equation.
proofs.scope: Strong induction on $|G|$; the trivial group has no prime divisor, so the induction needs no separate base case.

roles.why: Finiteness allows strong induction on $|G|$ and makes the class equation a finite count.
Primality gives Euclid's lemma: $p \mid ab$ forces $p \mid a$ or $p \mid b$.
Divisibility of $|G|$ by $p$ feeds every case of the induction.

steps.slogan: Prove the abelian case by induction through the quotient $G/\langle g \rangle$.
steps.detail: Take $g \ne e$ of order $m$. If $p \mid m$, then $g^{m/p}$ has order $p$. Otherwise $p$ divides $|G|/m = |G/\langle g \rangle|$, induction gives $h$ whose image has order $p$, so $p$ divides the order $k$ of $h$, and $h^{k/p}$ has order $p$.

steps.slogan: Write the class equation $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum_i [G : C_G(x_i)]$.
steps.detail: Conjugation splits $G$ into [conjugacy classes](c:conjugacy-class). Elements of the [center](c:center) $Z(G)$ form one-point classes, and the class of a noncentral $x_i$ has $[G : C_G(x_i)] > 1$ elements, so $C_G(x_i)$ is a proper subgroup.

steps.slogan: Apply induction to a proper centralizer whose order $p$ divides.
steps.detail: If $p$ divides $|C_G(x_i)|$ for some $i$, then $C_G(x_i)$ is a group of smaller order, so by induction it has an element of order $p$. That element lies in $G$.

steps.slogan: Otherwise show that $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$ and apply the abelian case.
steps.detail: If $p$ divides no $|C_G(x_i)|$, then $p$ divides each index $|G|/|C_G(x_i)|$ by Euclid's lemma. The class equation gives $p \mid |Z(G)|$, and the abelian case applied to $Z(G)$ gives an element of order $p$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two cases to complete the strong induction on $|G|$.
steps.detail: Either some proper centralizer has order divisible by $p$, or $p$ divides $|Z(G)|$. In both cases $G$ has an element of order $p$, so the statement holds for $G$.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness makes the counts and the induction possible.
concepts.c:prime-number: Only a prime forces orbit sizes or indices to behave this way.
concepts.c:order-of-an-element: The goal is an element whose order is exactly $p$.
concepts.c:conjugacy-class: Conjugacy classes are the orbits counted by the class equation.
concepts.c:center: The center is abelian, so the abelian case applies to it.

source.note: The classical induction proof through the class equation, as in I. N. Herstein, Topics in Algebra, chapter 2.

statement: For every $n \times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, the [characteristic polynomial](c:characteristic-polynomial) $p_A(t) = \det(tI_n - A)$ satisfies $p_A(A) = 0$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix) of size $n \times n$.
The entries of $A$ lie in a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$.

conclusion: Writing $p_A(t) = t^n + c_{n-1}t^{n-1} + \dots + c_0$, the matrix $A^n + c_{n-1}A^{n-1} + \dots + c_0 I_n$ is zero.

proofs.name: Adjugate and telescoping
proofs.slogan: Multiply $tI - A$ by its adjugate, compare the matrix coefficients of the powers of $t$, and let the sum telescope at $A$.
proofs.scope: Every $n \ge 0$ over every commutative ring; for $n = 0$ both sides are the empty matrix. The proof uses no division and no eigenvalues.

roles.why: A square matrix has a determinant and an adjugate.
Commutativity of $R$ and $R[t]$ makes the determinant and the identity $\operatorname{adj}(M)\, M = \det(M)\, I$ valid.

steps.slogan: Multiply $tI - A$ by its [adjugate](c:adjugate-matrix) over the [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[t]$.
steps.detail: Over the commutative ring $R[t]$, Laplace expansion gives $\operatorname{adj}(M)\, M = \det(M)\, I$ for every square matrix $M$. For $M = tI - A$ this reads $\operatorname{adj}(tI - A)(tI - A) = p_A(t)\, I$, since $p_A(t)$ is the [determinant](c:determinant) of $tI - A$.

steps.slogan: Compare the matrix coefficients of each power $t^k$ on both sides.
steps.detail: The entries of $\operatorname{adj}(tI - A)$ have degree below $n$, so $\operatorname{adj}(tI - A) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} B_k t^k$ with $B_k \in M_n(R)$. Comparing coefficients of $t^k$ gives $c_k I = B_{k-1} - B_k A$ for $0 \le k \le n$, with $B_{-1} = B_n = 0$ and $c_n = 1$.

steps.slogan: Multiply the $k$-th identity by $A^k$ on the right and add over all $k$.
steps.detail: Summing $c_k A^k = B_{k-1} A^k - B_k A^{k+1}$ over $k = 0, \dots, n$ gives $p_A(A)$ on the left. On the right the terms cancel in pairs because $B_{-1} = B_n = 0$, so $p_A(A) = 0$.

concepts.c:matrix: The theorem substitutes the matrix itself into a polynomial.
concepts.c:commutative-ring: Determinants and adjugates need commuting entries.
concepts.c:characteristic-polynomial: This is the polynomial that the matrix annihilates.
concepts.c:square-matrix: Only a square matrix has a characteristic polynomial.
concepts.c:adjugate-matrix: The adjugate supplies the factor $\sum_k B_k t^k$ of $p_A(t) I$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The identity is first proved with entries in $R[t]$.

source.note: mathlib starts from adjugate_mul, moves to polynomials with matrix coefficients through matPolyEquiv, and evaluates at $M$ with eval_mul_X_sub_C, which is the telescoping step.

statement: Let a group $G$ [act](c:group-action) on a set $X$, and choose one point $x_i$ in each [orbit](c:orbit). Then $X$ is in [bijection](c:bijection) with the disjoint union of the coset spaces $G/G_{x_i}$, where $G_{x_i}$ is the [stabilizer](c:stabilizer) of $x_i$. For finite $X$, $|X| = \sum_i [G : G_{x_i}]$.

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ [acts](c:group-action) on the set $X$.
For the counting formula, the set $X$ is finite.

conclusion: $X \cong \bigsqcup_i G/G_{x_i}$, and $|X| = \sum_i [G : G_{x_i}]$ when $X$ is finite.

formal.difference: The declaration is the bijection $X \simeq \Sigma_{\omega} G/G_{x_\omega}$ for representatives chosen by Quotient.out, with no finiteness. The counting form is MulAction.card_eq_sum_card_group_div_card_stabilizer, stated with $|G|/|G_x|$ for finite $G$.

proofs.name: Orbits and cosets
proofs.slogan: Split the set into orbits, match each orbit with the cosets of a stabilizer, and add the sizes.
proofs.scope: The bijection for every action, and the count for finite $X$. An empty $X$ has no orbits and gives the empty sum $0$.

roles.why: The action defines the orbits, the stabilizers and the map $g G_x \mapsto g \cdot x$.
Finiteness makes the orbit sizes finite numbers that add up to $|X|$.

steps.slogan: Show that lying in a common orbit is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation).
steps.detail: Put $x \sim y$ when $y = g \cdot x$ for some $g \in G$. The identity gives reflexivity, inverses give symmetry, and products give transitivity, because $h \cdot (g \cdot x) = (hg) \cdot x$.

steps.slogan: Write $X$ as the disjoint union of its orbits.
steps.detail: The equivalence classes of $\sim$ are the orbits $G \cdot x_i$, and they partition $X$. So $X$ is in bijection with the disjoint union $\bigsqcup_i G \cdot x_i$ over the chosen representatives.

steps.slogan: Match each orbit with the cosets of its stabilizer by $g G_{x_i} \mapsto g \cdot x_i$.
steps.detail: We have $g \cdot x_i = h \cdot x_i$ exactly when $h^{-1} g \in G_{x_i}$, that is when $g G_{x_i} = h G_{x_i}$. So the map is well defined and injective, and it is onto $G \cdot x_i$ by the definition of the orbit.

steps.slogan: Combine the bijections and count the elements of a finite $X$.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 3 give $X \cong \bigsqcup_i G/G_{x_i}$. For finite $X$ there are finitely many orbits, and $|G \cdot x_i|$ equals the [index](c:index-of-a-subgroup) $[G : G_{x_i}]$, so $|X| = \sum_i [G : G_{x_i}]$.

concepts.c:group-action: The action produces the orbits and stabilizers being counted.
concepts.c:orbit: Orbits are the blocks into which the set splits.
concepts.c:bijection: Each orbit matches the coset space one to one.
concepts.c:stabilizer: Cosets of the stabilizer label the points of an orbit.
concepts.c:equivalence-relation: Its classes are exactly the orbits.
concepts.c:index-of-a-subgroup: The index of the stabilizer is the orbit size.

source.note: mathlib composes the orbit decomposition selfEquivSigmaOrbits' with orbitEquivQuotientStabilizer on each orbit, through selfEquivSigmaOrbitsQuotientStabilizer'.

statement: Suppose a system runs through a cycle and takes heat $Q_i$ from reservoirs at absolute temperatures $T_i > 0$, with heat given off counted as negative. If the first and second laws of thermodynamics hold, then $\sum_i Q_i / T_i \le 0$; so the cyclic [line integral](c:line-integral) $\oint \delta Q / T$ is at most $0$, with equality for a reversible cycle.

hypotheses.text: The system runs through a closed cycle and returns to its initial state.
It exchanges heat $Q_i$ only with reservoirs at absolute temperatures $T_i > 0$.
The first law holds: over a cycle, the work done equals the net heat taken.
The Kelvin–Planck statement holds: no cyclic process turns heat from one reservoir into positive work and has no other effect.

conclusion: $\sum_i Q_i / T_i \le 0$, and in the continuous limit $\oint \delta Q / T \le 0$; a reversible cycle gives equality.

new_concepts.name: Carnot engine
new_concepts.reminder: A reversible heat engine that exchanges heat with two reservoirs only.
new_concepts.definition: A Carnot engine runs a reversible cycle that exchanges heat with exactly two reservoirs. If it takes heat $q_1$ at absolute temperature $t_1$ and heat $q_2$ at $t_2$, then $q_1/t_1 + q_2/t_2 = 0$; this relation defines the absolute temperature scale.

proofs.name: Auxiliary Carnot engines
proofs.slogan: Give each reservoir its heat back with a Carnot engine fed from one reference reservoir, then let the Kelvin–Planck statement forbid net work.
proofs.scope: Finitely many reservoirs in steps 1 to 4; step 5 passes to a continuous heat exchange as a limit of sums and treats the reversible case.

roles.why: A closed cycle makes the combined process cyclic, so every part returns to its initial state.
Positive reservoir temperatures let a Carnot engine run between each $T_i$ and $T_0$.
Energy balance over the cycle turns the net heat from the reference reservoir into work.
The Kelvin–Planck statement forbids positive work from a single reservoir.

steps.slogan: Add a reference reservoir at $T_0 > 0$ and one [Carnot engine](c:carnot-engine) for each reservoir.
steps.detail: Engine $C_i$ runs between $T_0$ and $T_i$ and gives the heat $Q_i$ back to reservoir $i$; it runs backward if $Q_i < 0$. By the Carnot relation it takes the heat $T_0 Q_i / T_i$ from the reference reservoir.

steps.slogan: Compute the net heat exchanges of the combined system over one cycle.
steps.detail: Each reservoir $T_i$ gets back exactly the heat $Q_i$ that the system took, so its net exchange is zero. The system and the engines return to their initial states, and the only net heat taken is $Q_0 = T_0 \sum_i Q_i / T_i$, from the reference reservoir.

steps.slogan: Equate the work of the combined cycle with the net heat $Q_0$.
steps.detail: Over a cycle the internal energy of the combined system returns to its initial value. The first law then says that the combined system does the work $W = Q_0$.

steps.slogan: Exclude positive work of the combined cycle by the Kelvin–Planck statement.
steps.detail: The combined cycle exchanges heat with the reference reservoir only, so the Kelvin–Planck statement forbids $W > 0$. So $T_0 \sum_i Q_i / T_i = W \le 0$, and $T_0 > 0$ gives $\sum_i Q_i / T_i \le 0$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the cyclic integral and treat reversible cycles.
steps.detail: For a continuous exchange, the sums of step 4 over finer splittings of the cycle are [Riemann sums](c:riemann-sum) of $\oint \delta Q / T$, so the integral is at most $0$. A reversible cycle run backward reverses the sign of every $Q_i$, which gives the opposite inequality and hence equality.

concepts.c:line-integral: The inequality concerns the cyclic integral of $\delta Q / T$.
concepts.c:carnot-engine: Auxiliary Carnot engines move all heat exchange to one reservoir.
concepts.c:riemann-sum: Finite reservoir sums approximate the cyclic integral.

source.note: The classical proof with auxiliary Carnot cycles, as in E. Fermi, Thermodynamics (1936), chapter IV.

statement: A set $T$ of [first-order](c:first-order-logic) [sentences](c:sentence) has a [model](c:model) if and only if every finite subset of $T$ has a model.

hypotheses.text: $T$ is a set of first-order [sentences](c:sentence) in some language $L$.

conclusion: $T$ is satisfiable exactly when it is finitely satisfiable.

proofs.name: Ultraproduct of finite models
proofs.slogan: Take a model of each finite subset, glue the models by an ultraproduct along an ultrafilter that eventually contains each sentence, and apply Łoś's theorem.
proofs.scope: Both directions; the forward direction is immediate. Structures are nonempty, and an empty $T$ gets the model chosen for its only finite subset $\emptyset$.

roles.why: First-order sentences are exactly what Łoś's theorem transfers to the ultraproduct.

steps.slogan: Reuse a model of $T$ as a model of each finite subset.
steps.detail: A structure that satisfies every sentence of $T$ satisfies every sentence of each subset of $T$. So a model of $T$ is a model of each finite subset.

steps.slogan: Choose a model $M_\Delta$ for each finite subset $\Delta \subseteq T$.
steps.detail: Let $I$ be the set of finite subsets of $T$. Finite satisfiability gives, for each $\Delta \in I$, a structure $M_\Delta$ that satisfies every sentence of $\Delta$; the axiom of choice picks one for each $\Delta$.

steps.slogan: Extend the sets $\{\Delta : \Delta \supseteq \Delta_0\}$ to an [ultrafilter](c:ultrafilter) $U$ on $I$.
steps.detail: The sets $\uparrow\Delta_0 = \{\Delta \in I : \Delta \supseteq \Delta_0\}$ are nonempty and $\uparrow\Delta_0 \cap \uparrow\Delta_1 = \uparrow(\Delta_0 \cup \Delta_1)$, so they have the [finite intersection property](c:finite-intersection-property). The ultrafilter theorem extends them to an ultrafilter $U$ on $I$.

steps.slogan: Form the [ultraproduct](c:ultraproduct) $M = \prod_\Delta M_\Delta / U$.
steps.detail: Take families $(a_\Delta)$ with $a_\Delta \in M_\Delta$ and identify two of them when they agree on a set in $U$. Functions act coordinatewise, and a relation holds in $M$ when it holds on a set in $U$.

steps.slogan: Transfer each sentence of $T$ to the ultraproduct by Łoś's theorem.
steps.detail: Łoś's theorem says that $M \models \varphi$ exactly when $\{\Delta : M_\Delta \models \varphi\} \in U$. For $\varphi \in T$ this set contains $\uparrow\{\varphi\}$, which lies in $U$, so $M \models \varphi$. Hence $M$ is a model of $T$.

steps.slogan: Combine both directions into the stated equivalence.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives finite satisfiability from satisfiability. Steps 2 to 5 build a model of $T$ from models of its finite subsets, so the two properties are equivalent.

concepts.c:first-order-logic: Łoś's theorem holds for first-order formulas, not for stronger logics.
concepts.c:sentence: Satisfaction of sentences is what passes to the ultraproduct.
concepts.c:model: The proof builds a model of $T$ from models of finite parts.
concepts.c:ultrafilter: The ultrafilter decides which coordinates count as almost all.
concepts.c:finite-intersection-property: It lets the sets $\uparrow\Delta_0$ extend to an ultrafilter.
concepts.c:ultraproduct: The ultraproduct glues the finite models into one structure.

source.note: mathlib picks a model of each finite subset, forms Filter.Product along Ultrafilter.of atTop on the finite subsets, and applies Ultraproduct.sentence_realize, which is Łoś's theorem.

statement: Let $F\colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$ whose [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) has constant [rank](c:rank-of-a-matrix) $r$. Then each $p \in U$ has [diffeomorphisms](c:diffeomorph) $\varphi$ near $p$ and $\psi$ near $F(p)$ with $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}(x_1, \dots, x_m) = (x_1, \dots, x_r, 0, \dots, 0)$.

hypotheses.text: $F\colon U \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is a [smooth map](c:smooth-map) on an open set $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}^m$.
The [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) $DF(x)$ has the same [rank](c:rank-of-a-matrix) $r$ at every $x \in U$.

conclusion: Near each point, after smooth changes of coordinates in the source and the target, $F$ is the linear projection $(x_1, \dots, x_m) \mapsto (x_1, \dots, x_r, 0, \dots, 0)$.

proofs.name: Two coordinate changes
proofs.slogan: Straighten the first $r$ components of $F$ by the inverse function theorem, use constant rank to kill the dependence on the other variables, then straighten the image.
proofs.scope: The local statement at one point $p$; all neighborhoods may shrink. For $r = 0$ the map is locally constant, and $r = m$ or $r = n$ give the immersion and submersion theorems.

roles.why: Smoothness lets the inverse function theorem apply to $\varphi$ and keeps every map smooth.
Rank $r$ at $p$ gives the invertible block; rank $r$ near $p$ kills $\partial \tilde R / \partial v$.

steps.slogan: Reorder the coordinates so that the top-left $r \times r$ block of $DF(p)$ is invertible.
steps.detail: Since $DF(p)$ has rank $r$, it has an invertible $r \times r$ minor, and permutations of coordinates move it to the top left. Write $x = (u, v) \in \mathbb{R}^r \times \mathbb{R}^{m-r}$ and $F = (Q, R)$ with $Q$ the first $r$ components.

steps.slogan: Straighten the first $r$ components with the map $\varphi(u, v) = (Q(u, v), v)$.
steps.detail: The [Jacobian matrix](c:jacobian-matrix) of $\varphi$ at $p$ is block triangular with the invertible block $\partial Q / \partial u$ and the identity, so it is invertible. The inverse function theorem makes $\varphi$ a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) near $p$, and $F \circ \varphi^{-1}(y, v) = (y, \tilde R(y, v))$ for a smooth $\tilde R$.

steps.slogan: Show from the constant rank that $\tilde R$ does not depend on $v$.
steps.detail: The Jacobian of $F \circ \varphi^{-1}$ has the blocks $I_r$, $0$, $\partial \tilde R / \partial y$ and $\partial \tilde R / \partial v$, and its rank is $r$ because $\varphi$ is a diffeomorphism. A nonzero entry of $\partial \tilde R / \partial v$ would give rank $r + 1$, so $\tilde R(y, v) = S(y)$ on a product neighborhood.

steps.slogan: Straighten the image with the map $\psi(y, z) = (y, z - S(y))$.
steps.detail: The map $\psi$ is a diffeomorphism with inverse $(y, w) \mapsto (y, w + S(y))$. Then $\psi \circ F \circ \varphi^{-1}(y, v) = (y, S(y) - S(y)) = (y, 0)$, which is the stated normal form.

concepts.c:smooth-map: Smoothness is needed for the inverse function theorem.
concepts.c:jacobian-matrix: Its block form controls both coordinate changes.
concepts.c:rank-of-a-matrix: Constant rank forces the extra block to vanish.
concepts.c:diffeomorph: The coordinate changes are diffeomorphisms near $p$ and $F(p)$.

source.note: The standard proof from the inverse function theorem, as in J. M. Lee, Introduction to Smooth Manifolds, 2nd ed., theorem 4.12 (the rank theorem).

statement: Let $X$ be a [topological space](c:topological-space) and $(Y, d)$ a [metric space](c:metric-space). If [continuous](c:continuous-function) functions $f_n\colon X \to Y$ [converge uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) to $f$, then $f$ is continuous.

hypotheses.text: Each $f_n\colon X \to Y$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).
The functions $f_n$ converge [uniformly](c:uniform-convergence) to $f$: $\sup_{x \in X} d(f_n(x), f(x)) \to 0$.

conclusion: The limit function $f$ is continuous on $X$.

formal.difference: The declaration allows any uniform space $Y$ and asks only that for each entourage some continuous function lies uniformly close to $f$, which a uniformly convergent sequence supplies.

proofs.name: Three-epsilon estimate
proofs.slogan: Approximate $f$ uniformly by one continuous $f_N$, use the continuity of $f_N$ at the point, and add three small distances.
proofs.scope: Continuity at an arbitrary point $x_0 \in X$, which gives continuity on all of $X$.

roles.why: Uniform convergence gives one $f_N$ within $\varepsilon/3$ of $f$ at every point.
Continuity of $f_N$ at $x_0$ gives the neighborhood of the estimate.

steps.slogan: Choose one index $N$ with $f_N$ uniformly within $\varepsilon/3$ of $f$.
steps.detail: Fix $x_0 \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Uniform convergence gives $N$ with $d(f_N(x), f(x)) < \varepsilon/3$ for every $x \in X$ at once.

steps.slogan: Find a [neighborhood](c:neighborhood) of $x_0$ on which $f_N$ varies by less than $\varepsilon/3$.
steps.detail: The function $f_N$ is continuous at $x_0$, so some open neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ has $d(f_N(x), f_N(x_0)) < \varepsilon/3$ for all $x \in V$.

steps.slogan: Add the three distances on $V$ by the triangle inequality.
steps.detail: For $x \in V$, $d(f(x), f(x_0)) \le d(f(x), f_N(x)) + d(f_N(x), f_N(x_0)) + d(f_N(x_0), f(x_0)) < \varepsilon$. Since $x_0$ and $\varepsilon$ are arbitrary, $f$ is continuous.

concepts.c:topological-space: Continuity on $X$ needs only neighborhoods, not a metric.
concepts.c:metric-space: Distances in $Y$ are split into three small parts.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity of one approximant carries over to the limit.
concepts.c:uniform-convergence: One index $N$ must work at every point simultaneously.
concepts.c:neighborhood: The neighborhood of $x_0$ comes from continuity of $f_N$.

source.note: mathlib reduces to continuousWithinAt_of_locally_uniform_approx_of_continuousWithinAt, which takes a symmetric entourage whose triple composite lies in the given one: the uniform-space form of the three $\varepsilon/3$ terms.

statement: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ whose [determinant](c:determinant) is a [unit](c:unit), for example a nonzero real number, and let $b \in R^n$. The [linear system](c:system-of-linear-equations) $Ax = b$ has exactly one solution, $x_i = \det A_i / \det A$, where $A_i$ is $A$ with column $i$ replaced by $b$.

hypotheses.text: $A$ is an $n \times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$, and $b \in R^n$.
The [determinant](c:determinant) $\det A$ is a [unit](c:unit) of $R$.

conclusion: The unique solution of $Ax = b$ is $x_i = \det A_i / \det A$ for $i = 1, \dots, n$.

formal.difference: The declaration states $A\,x = (\det A)\, b$ for the vector $x_i = \det A_i$, with no hypothesis on $\det A$. Division by $\det A$ and uniqueness of the solution are not part of it.

proofs.name: Adjugate identity
proofs.slogan: Identify the Cramer vector with the adjugate times $b$, use $A \operatorname{adj}(A) = (\det A) I$, and divide by the determinant.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness for every $n \ge 1$; for $n = 0$ both sides are the empty vector.

roles.why: A square matrix over a commutative ring has a determinant, cofactors and an adjugate.
Invertibility of $\det A$ allows the division in both directions.

steps.slogan: Expand $\det A_i$ along column $i$ to get the $i$-th entry of $\operatorname{adj}(A)\, b$.
steps.detail: Laplace expansion along column $i$ gives $\det A_i = \sum_j b_j C_{ji}$, where $C_{ji}$ is the cofactor of $A$ at $(j, i)$. The [adjugate](c:adjugate-matrix) has $(i, j)$ entry $C_{ji}$, so the vector $(\det A_i)_i$ equals $\operatorname{adj}(A)\, b$.

steps.slogan: Show that $A \operatorname{adj}(A) = \operatorname{adj}(A)\, A = (\det A)\, I$.
steps.detail: The $(k, i)$ entry of $A \operatorname{adj}(A)$ is $\sum_j a_{kj} C_{ij}$, the Laplace expansion along row $i$ of $A$ with row $i$ replaced by row $k$. It is $\det A$ for $k = i$ and $0$ for $k \ne i$, since a matrix with two equal rows has determinant $0$; columns give the other product.

steps.slogan: Divide by $\det A$ to obtain a solution of $Ax = b$.
steps.detail: Steps 1 and 2 give $A\, (\det A_i)_i = A \operatorname{adj}(A)\, b = (\det A)\, b$. Multiplication by $(\det A)^{-1}$ shows that $x_i = \det A_i / \det A$ solves $Ax = b$.

steps.slogan: Show that every solution equals the solution of step 3.
steps.detail: If $Ax = b$, then $(\det A)\, x = \operatorname{adj}(A) A x = \operatorname{adj}(A)\, b = (\det A_i)_i$ by steps 1 and 2. Division by $\det A$ gives $x_i = \det A_i / \det A$, so the solution of step 3 is the only one.

concepts.c:matrix: The coefficients of the system form a square matrix.
concepts.c:determinant: Each unknown is a quotient of two determinants.
concepts.c:unit: Division by the determinant needs it to be invertible.
concepts.c:system-of-linear-equations: The rule solves the square system $Ax = b$.
concepts.c:adjugate-matrix: The adjugate times $b$ is the vector of numerators.
